newsitem.title: GUYANA: Guyana posts 7.9 percent growth in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Guyana posts 7.9 percent growth in 1996.

text.p: Guyanese Finance Minister Bharrat Jagdeo said Friday the economy grew 7.9 percent in 1996, up from 5.1 percent in 1995, and was set to maintain a seven percent clip this year -- one of the highest forecast for the region.

While presenting the 1997 budget to parliament, Jagdeo said even as the economy generated "a growth rate, one of the highest in the region," inflation fell to 4.5 percent compared to 8.1 percent in 1995.

Jagdeo said inflation's fall to its lowest level since 1972 had been helped by "declining inflation in partner countries, a fairly stable exchange rate, increased competition and prudent fiscal and monetary policies."

Although still one of Latin America's poorest nations, the former British colony has enjoyed a relative economic boom in recent years after two decades of state control and socialist experiments sent it on a steady downhill slide.
Last year's growth "performance is even more heartening when one takes into account the extensive flooding throughout the country last year which damaged both crops and livestock," Jagdeo said.
Rice output grew 6.1 percent to 334,515 tonnes, sugar production rose to its highest level in 14 years at 334,525 tonnes, while manufacturing rose 3.0 percent.

In the mining sector, declared gold production amounted to 372,000 ounces, 29 percent above 1995, while bauxite production rose 16.7 percent to 2,367,670 tonnes, led by increases in metallurgic and chemical grade bauxite.
The stock of external debt was meanwhile reduced by more than $617 million, as direct foreign investment increased about ten percent versus a net outflow of short term capital of $2.7 million.
"Inflows from external sources of $120 million were probably the highest ever," Jagdeo told lawmakers.
Exports grew by 13.9 percent to $565 million, led by sugar, gold and forestry, while imports grew 9.7 percent to $589 million.
Jagdeo said this resulted in an improvement in the trade deficit of $17 million over the previous year, while scheduled interest payments fell some $7 million to $79 million.

With a population of 800,000 -- and as many living outside the country, mostly in the United States, Canada and Britain -- Guyana recently implemented major recent economic reforms supported by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
In May the country won a major agreement from the Paris Club of creditor nations to reduce by 67 percent its $2.1 billion foreign debt -- then the highest debt per capita burden in the world.
